chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
title: The Zanzibar and Roxy show with Bill Robinson
summary: Glaser tested McRae with the Zanzibar show, which he rehearsed with Bill Robinson's act in Washington and doubled with the Roxy.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: He books me into the Zanzibar. Remember the Zanzibar in New York? It was a big show. Now here's the show we had at the Zanzibar.
We had Louie Armstrong and his band, Mr. Bill Robinson, The Delta Rhythm Boys, The Peter Sisters, Maurice Rocco, and the Nicholas Kids. Now that's enough show to run you crazy.
Claude Hopkins in the Zanzibar. We're coming out of Washinton, D.C.. We come in there Friday morning at 9:00
Mr. Howard, who owns the place, say, 'Are you gonna open the show today?'
'Yeah, I'm going to open up tonight. I want a 5:30 dress.' This is all on me. The road

manager, Joe Glaser -- nobody can tell me nothing. All he did -- Joe Glaser signed the contract. Louie going to open tonight. This is the show. The show is all set.
Meanwhile, Claude Hopkins and Ellie Hill, arranger -- big arranger on Broadway at that time -- they were doing the music to the show.
Alec Hill
(Inaudible)?
(Inaudible)?
Yeah. Not Ellie, another Hill. He was a very big arranger. He wrote for a lot of acts and things on Broadway at the time.
They were doing the music for the Zanzibar show.
So in the meanwhile, they come to Washington during the week, and Bill Robinson came down with them.
Bill Robinson had very hard music. It was the most beautiful music you ever heard outside of Bert Williams years ago.
He had very good music -- technical. Of course, you know Bill Robinson was
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
a very good dancer. And his music fit to everything that he's doing. It was like, pretty, soft, and everything.
At that time, I was playing bass clarinet and everything. So I said, "Okay."
He came down to Washington so -- We were playing the Howard Theater.
So after the last show -- the picture went off about one o'clock, we came back twelve o'clock. We came back to rehearse the show that we was going to do in the Zanzibar.
We're going to rehearse the opening number and rehearse Bill Robinson's music. I'm going to clean up his act -- going to do his act.

Not going to rehearse it in New York. I'm going to rehearse his act here. I say, "Now, Bill, I'm going to rehearse your act and I'm going to clean it up. You're going to do your act here, and I won't have to do it in New York. Because I have a lot of work to do when I get to New York."
I says -- Claude says, "I'll take the band down on the opening." So he get up on the

bandstand, pass out the music. He took the band down on what they were supposed to do as an opening in the Zanzibar.
They ran down the opening and a part of the finale and part -- skimmed over part of picture, (inaudible) girls, come up with bands and all that stuff.
So I say, "Okay. Give me Bill." I say, "I'll take (inaudible)."
So I took Bill's music down (inaudible). "(Inaudible) played my music down the first time right."

Because when Bill was sitting there, I said, I'll be with you in a minute," because I was going through the arrangements -- showing the fellas in the band little spots that I wanted -- "Play that little bar down there, the that A and D 32nd bar, (inaudible)." Two (Inaudible) bars and I go over that little spot here and a little spot there. I say, "Okay, let's take it down.
Bill come up on the stage and say, "What's

the tempo?" He give me the tempo. "This the tempo, fellas. When we give the introduction, stop."
"Do it one more time, Good (inaudible), stop. That's fine, let's do it. Take it down."
Then we go straight through it -- I went through it. Bill says, "That's fine, let's do the next number."
Get the tempo on that. Try that down a couple of times, we go on down through it.
Once I got Bill Robinson's tempos, that's all I needed. I'm not gonna change it, I know those tempos.
See, once you give me the tempo, ah, that's the tempo. I know your tempo, right?
So we get to New York, Van (inaudible). I say, "Why you fellas sitting up here so early in the morning?"
"Well we thought we're going to play the show. Somebody said your band couldn't read."
(Inaudible).

Because they put all the music up on the bandstand. Claude say, "I'm gonna tell you how it go."
I say, "No, you can't tell my band," you know. Put the (Inaudible) music here. You tell me and I'll tell the band. This is my band. You don't" -- even Louie don't talk to this band.
I say, "I don't want to blow them to death." I say, "Look, just take it down with the rhythm section."
"Just take it down with the rhythm section. Swanson could play it." Very good piano player.
"Just take it down with the rhythm section and just skim through it and see if the music isn't too long, what we got to cut out the music and so and so."
We took the opening down. And we got it down. We tried it down (inaudible) with the band, then we took it down with the girls.
Now when were running the thing down, they
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

had too much music. So I stopped and we cut out, and we trimmed it down. We took act after act. After that, went through the middle number, went through the last number, the opening number, the closing number, and we were ready for a dress at 5:30.
And we doubled out of the Zanzibar into the Roxy doing five shows in the Roxy, and three shows in the Zanzibar.
That was enough for anybody. That was some hard work.
Imagine playing three long shows in he Zanzibar. In the meanwhile you're doing from 12 o'clock to 12 o'clock at the Roxy -- you're doing five shows over there.
And packed everyday with Bill Robinson, Louie Armstrong, Delta Rhythm Boys, the Peter Sisters, Nicholas Kids. Some show.
So that all have to come through you. You got to do all that. Put it altogether -- everything. Handle the musicians, handle the arrangers and --
Handle the musicians --
I needed another tenor
player so I brought in Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis to play the hot tenor so I could (inaudible) conduct the band.
